Text: How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: Are the first year's suggested courses different for a BA vs BS in Computer Science?
answer:
Yes. The first-year suggested courses are different for the Bachelor of Arts in Computer Science and the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science.

For the B.S. in Computer Science, the freshman suggested plan assumes placement into MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I and ENGL 1110G Composition I. The first year includes CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2230 Assembly Language and Machine Organization, ENGL 1110G Composition I, MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, MATH 1521G Calculus and Analytic Geometry II, an Area IV Social/Behavioral Sciences course, and an Area V Humanities course, for 30 credits.

For the B.A. in Computer Science, the freshman suggested plan assumes placement into MATH 1220G College Algebra and ENGL 1110G Composition I. The first year includes CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles, ENGL 1110G Composition I, MATH 1220G College Algebra, COMM 1115G Introduction to Communication, CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I or MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I, an Area III Laboratory Science course, an Area IV Social/Behavioral Sciences course, and elective credits as needed for financial aid, for 30–32 credits.

Both plans say the order can vary depending on initial math and English placement, and the plans are suggestions rather than contracts.

Text: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is the traditional undergraduate degree in Computer Science. It is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of Computer Science. It prepares the student for any technological ﬁeld in industry, and also provides the preparation for graduate studies in Computer Science. It is the main undergraduate degree in the Computer Science department, and should be the choice of a single-major Computer Science student. This degree is accredited by the ABET Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria. General Requirements Exception A grade of at least C- must be earned in each of the courses taken to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. No course may be counted as satisfying both a departmental and a non-departmental requirement. No course taken to satisfy either a departmental or a non-departmental requirement may be taken S/U. Requirements Students who plan to seek employment at the bachelor level are advised to take one of the concentration area curricula in addition to the general and departmental requirements. An elective course cannot be used for more than two focuses. A course that is required for one concentration cannot be used as an elective course of another one. Students must complete all University degree requirements, which include: General Education requirements, Viewing a Wider World requirements, and elective credits to total at least 120 credits with 48 credits in courses numbered 300/3000 or above. Developmental coursework will not count towards the degree requirements and/or elective credits, but may be needed in order to take the necessary English and Mathematics coursework. Text: How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: Are the first year's suggested courses different for a BA vs BS in Computer Science?
answer:
Yes. The first-year suggested courses are different for the Bachelor of Arts in Computer Science and the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science.

For the B.S. in Computer Science, the freshman suggested plan assumes placement into MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I and ENGL 1110G Composition I. The first year includes CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2230 Assembly Language and Machine Organization, ENGL 1110G Composition I, MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, MATH 1521G Calculus and Analytic Geometry II, an Area IV Social/Behavioral Sciences course, and an Area V Humanities course, for 30 credits.

For the B.A. in Computer Science, the freshman suggested plan assumes placement into MATH 1220G College Algebra and ENGL 1110G Composition I. The first year includes CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles, ENGL 1110G Composition I, MATH 1220G College Algebra, COMM 1115G Introduction to Communication, CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I or MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I, an Area III Laboratory Science course, an Area IV Social/Behavioral Sciences course, and elective credits as needed for financial aid, for 30–32 credits.

Both plans say the order can vary depending on initial math and English placement, and the plans are suggestions rather than contracts.

Text: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is the traditional undergraduate degree in Computer Science. It is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of Computer Science. It prepares the student for any technological ﬁeld in industry, and also provides the preparation for graduate studies in Computer Science. It is the main undergraduate degree in the Computer Science department, and should be the choice of a single-major Computer Science student. This degree is accredited by the ABET Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria. General Requirements Exception A grade of at least C- must be earned in each of the courses taken to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. No course may be counted as satisfying both a departmental and a non-departmental requirement. No course taken to satisfy either a departmental or a non-departmental requirement may be taken S/U. Requirements Students who plan to seek employment at the bachelor level are advised to take one of the concentration area curricula in addition to the general and departmental requirements. An elective course cannot be used for more than two focuses. A course that is required for one concentration cannot be used as an elective course of another one. Students must complete all University degree requirements, which include: General Education requirements, Viewing a Wider World requirements, and elective credits to total at least 120 credits with 48 credits in courses numbered 300/3000 or above. Developmental coursework will not count towards the degree requirements and/or elective credits, but may be needed in order to take the necessary English and Mathematics coursework. The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: Are the first year's suggested courses different for a BA vs BS in Computer Science?
answer:
Yes. The first-year suggested courses are different for the Bachelor of Arts in Computer Science and the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science.

For the B.S. in Computer Science, the freshman suggested plan assumes placement into MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I and ENGL 1110G Composition I. The first year includes CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2230 Assembly Language and Machine Organization, ENGL 1110G Composition I, MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, MATH 1521G Calculus and Analytic Geometry II, an Area IV Social/Behavioral Sciences course, and an Area V Humanities course, for 30 credits.

For the B.A. in Computer Science, the freshman suggested plan assumes placement into MATH 1220G College Algebra and ENGL 1110G Composition I. The first year includes CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles, ENGL 1110G Composition I, MATH 1220G College Algebra, COMM 1115G Introduction to Communication, CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I or MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I, an Area III Laboratory Science course, an Area IV Social/Behavioral Sciences course, and elective credits as needed for financial aid, for 30–32 credits.

Both plans say the order can vary depending on initial math and English placement, and the plans are suggestions rather than contracts.

Text: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is the traditional undergraduate degree in Computer Science. It is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of Computer Science. It prepares the student for any technological ﬁeld in industry, and also provides the preparation for graduate studies in Computer Science. It is the main undergraduate degree in the Computer Science department, and should be the choice of a single-major Computer Science student. This degree is accredited by the ABET Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria. General Requirements Exception A grade of at least C- must be earned in each of the courses taken to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. No course may be counted as satisfying both a departmental and a non-departmental requirement. No course taken to satisfy either a departmental or a non-departmental requirement may be taken S/U. Requirements Students who plan to seek employment at the bachelor level are advised to take one of the concentration area curricula in addition to the general and departmental requirements. An elective course cannot be used for more than two focuses. A course that is required for one concentration cannot be used as an elective course of another one. Students must complete all University degree requirements, which include: General Education requirements, Viewing a Wider World requirements, and elective credits to total at least 120 credits with 48 credits in courses numbered 300/3000 or above. Developmental coursework will not count towards the degree requirements and/or elective credits, but may be needed in order to take the necessary English and Mathematics coursework. Text: How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: Are the first year's suggested courses different for a BA vs BS in Computer Science?
answer:
Yes. The first-year suggested courses are different for the Bachelor of Arts in Computer Science and the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science.

For the B.S. in Computer Science, the freshman suggested plan assumes placement into MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I and ENGL 1110G Composition I. The first year includes CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2230 Assembly Language and Machine Organization, ENGL 1110G Composition I, MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, MATH 1521G Calculus and Analytic Geometry II, an Area IV Social/Behavioral Sciences course, and an Area V Humanities course, for 30 credits.

For the B.A. in Computer Science, the freshman suggested plan assumes placement into MATH 1220G College Algebra and ENGL 1110G Composition I. The first year includes CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles, ENGL 1110G Composition I, MATH 1220G College Algebra, COMM 1115G Introduction to Communication, CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I or MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I, an Area III Laboratory Science course, an Area IV Social/Behavioral Sciences course, and elective credits as needed for financial aid, for 30–32 credits.

Both plans say the order can vary depending on initial math and English placement, and the plans are suggestions rather than contracts.

Text: How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: Are the first year's suggested courses different for a BA vs BS in Computer Science?
answer:
Yes. The first-year suggested courses are different for the Bachelor of Arts in Computer Science and the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science.

For the B.S. in Computer Science, the freshman suggested plan assumes placement into MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I and ENGL 1110G Composition I. The first year includes CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2230 Assembly Language and Machine Organization, ENGL 1110G Composition I, MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, MATH 1521G Calculus and Analytic Geometry II, an Area IV Social/Behavioral Sciences course, and an Area V Humanities course, for 30 credits.

For the B.A. in Computer Science, the freshman suggested plan assumes placement into MATH 1220G College Algebra and ENGL 1110G Composition I. The first year includes CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles, ENGL 1110G Composition I, MATH 1220G College Algebra, COMM 1115G Introduction to Communication, CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I or MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I, an Area III Laboratory Science course, an Area IV Social/Behavioral Sciences course, and elective credits as needed for financial aid, for 30–32 credits.

Both plans say the order can vary depending on initial math and English placement, and the plans are suggestions rather than contracts.

Text: How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: Would I enroll in the same classes my first semester whether I was seeking a BS or a BA in computer science?
answer:
Not necessarily. The first CS course can be the same, because both the B.S. and B.A. in Computer Science include CSCI 1720 Computer Science I as part of the degree requirements.

The main difference is that the B.S. is more prescribed in math and science. The B.S. requires MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, while the B.A. allows either MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I or MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I. The B.S. also has more specific lab science and additional math requirements, while the B.A. is more flexible and leaves more room for coursework outside Computer Science.

So your first semester might look very similar in the two programs, especially if you take CSCI 1720 Computer Science I and MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I. But it would not automatically be the same; the B.A. gives you more flexibility, and your exact schedule would depend on placement, completed credits, and advising.

It is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of Computer Science. It prepares the student for any technological ﬁeld in industry, and also provides the preparation for graduate studies in Computer Science. An elective course cannot be used for more than two focuses. A course that is required for one concentration cannot be used as an elective course of another one. The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: Would I enroll in the same classes my first semester whether I was seeking a BS or a BA in computer science?
answer:
Not necessarily. The first CS course can be the same, because both the B.S. and B.A. in Computer Science include CSCI 1720 Computer Science I as part of the degree requirements.

The main difference is that the B.S. is more prescribed in math and science. The B.S. requires MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, while the B.A. allows either MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I or MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I. The B.S. also has more specific lab science and additional math requirements, while the B.A. is more flexible and leaves more room for coursework outside Computer Science.

So your first semester might look very similar in the two programs, especially if you take CSCI 1720 Computer Science I and MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I. But it would not automatically be the same; the B.A. gives you more flexibility, and your exact schedule would depend on placement, completed credits, and advising.

question: Would I enroll in the same classes my first semester whether I was seeking a BS or a BA in computer science?
answer:
Not necessarily. The first CS course can be the same, because both the B.S. and B.A. in Computer Science include CSCI 1720 Computer Science I as part of the degree requirements.

The main difference is that the B.S. is more prescribed in math and science. The B.S. requires MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, while the B.A. allows either MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I or MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I. The B.S. also has more specific lab science and additional math requirements, while the B.A. is more flexible and leaves more room for coursework outside Computer Science.

So your first semester might look very similar in the two programs, especially if you take CSCI 1720 Computer Science I and MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I. But it would not automatically be the same; the B.A. gives you more flexibility, and your exact schedule would depend on placement, completed credits, and advising.

question: Would I enroll in the same classes my first semester whether I was seeking a BS or a BA in computer science?
answer:
Not necessarily. The first CS course can be the same, because both the B.S. and B.A. in Computer Science include CSCI 1720 Computer Science I as part of the degree requirements.

The main difference is that the B.S. is more prescribed in math and science. The B.S. requires MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, while the B.A. allows either MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I or MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I. The B.S. also has more specific lab science and additional math requirements, while the B.A. is more flexible and leaves more room for coursework outside Computer Science.

So your first semester might look very similar in the two programs, especially if you take CSCI 1720 Computer Science I and MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I. But it would not automatically be the same; the B.A. gives you more flexibility, and your exact schedule would depend on placement, completed credits, and advising.

Text: How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: Would I enroll in the same classes my first semester whether I was seeking a BS or a BA in computer science?
answer:
Not necessarily. The first CS course can be the same, because both the B.S. and B.A. in Computer Science include CSCI 1720 Computer Science I as part of the degree requirements.

The main difference is that the B.S. is more prescribed in math and science. The B.S. requires MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, while the B.A. allows either MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I or MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I. The B.S. also has more specific lab science and additional math requirements, while the B.A. is more flexible and leaves more room for coursework outside Computer Science.

So your first semester might look very similar in the two programs, especially if you take CSCI 1720 Computer Science I and MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I. But it would not automatically be the same; the B.A. gives you more flexibility, and your exact schedule would depend on placement, completed credits, and advising.

Text: The Computer Science Department facilities have evolved from a single mainframe computing environment to a heterogeneous system of distributed workstations The department has workstations and servers running Linux, Solaris, MacOS, and Windows all connected by a segmented Gigabit ethernet network The J Mack Adams undergraduate lab is based on high-end PC hardware running 64bit Linux operating system At present, the lab consists of 63 HP and Acer MultiCores workstations Two laser printers for classwork purposes are also available SH 118B classroom has been built out of part of the J Mack Adams lab, and has 40 HP notebooks running 64bit Suse Linux The classroom also has three fixed LCD projectors which project onto a writeable surface and are controlled from an instructor’s console The graduate student lab has high-end Intel machines running 64 bit Suse Linux, and laser printing facilities Many graduate students also share computing resources with their advising faculty members in special-purpose laboratories In addition, every graduate student with an office has one Windows, Mac or Linux host for access to the shared computing facilities of the department The research facilities of the department consist of a great variety of machines located in faculty offices, graduate and special purpose labs These include many PC-based platforms (running a variety of operating systems), as well as several special-purpose parallel computing platforms including a Sun v890 SMP, multi-processor Sun workstations, small clusters and a large cluster consiting of 192 processor cores The Computer Operations Group (COG) operates the department’s computing facilities A large body of software is installed and maintained by this group, and direct support is provided for research projects through identification, acquisition, installation and consulting for a wide variety of software and hardware products

Text: The Mission of the Computer Science Department is to provide formal education in the core disciplines of computer science, as well as to prepare our graduates for research, development and academic careers. The department offers specific expertise in several research areas, such as bioinformatics, artificial intelligence and knowledge representation, software engineering and programming languages, computer and wireless networks, data mining and machine learning, game design and human-computer interaction, high performance computing, theory of computing, computer architectures, and assistive technologies. A number of laboratories have been established to coordinate research activities, including the Knowledge representation, Logic and Advanced Programming (KLAP) laboratory, the Programming Languages, Environments, and Automated Software Engineering (PLEASE) laboratory, the Play and Interactive Experiences for Learning (PIxL) lab, the Database Management and Data Mining laboratory, and the Network and Systems Optimization laboratory. The Department members are also directing the CREST Center for Research Excellence in Bioinformatics and Computational Biology, offering educational and research opportunities in bioinformatics.

Text: The Computer Science Department facilities have evolved from a single mainframe computing environment to a heterogeneous system of distributed workstations The department has workstations and servers running Linux, Solaris, MacOS, and Windows all connected by a segmented Gigabit ethernet network The J Mack Adams undergraduate lab is based on high-end PC hardware running 64bit Linux operating system At present, the lab consists of 63 HP and Acer MultiCores workstations Two laser printers for classwork purposes are also available SH 118B classroom has been built out of part of the J Mack Adams lab, and has 40 HP notebooks running 64bit Suse Linux The classroom also has three fixed LCD projectors which project onto a writeable surface and are controlled from an instructor’s console The graduate student lab has high-end Intel machines running 64 bit Suse Linux, and laser printing facilities Many graduate students also share computing resources with their advising faculty members in special-purpose laboratories In addition, every graduate student with an office has one Windows, Mac or Linux host for access to the shared computing facilities of the department The research facilities of the department consist of a great variety of machines located in faculty offices, graduate and special purpose labs These include many PC-based platforms (running a variety of operating systems), as well as several special-purpose parallel computing platforms including a Sun v890 SMP, multi-processor Sun workstations, small clusters and a large cluster consiting of 192 processor cores The Computer Operations Group (COG) operates the department’s computing facilities A large body of software is installed and maintained by this group, and direct support is provided for research projects through identification, acquisition, installation and consulting for a wide variety of software and hardware products

Text: The Computer Science Department facilities have evolved from a single mainframe computing environment to a heterogeneous system of distributed workstations The department has workstations and servers running Linux, Solaris, MacOS, and Windows all connected by a segmented Gigabit ethernet network The J Mack Adams undergraduate lab is based on high-end PC hardware running 64bit Linux operating system At present, the lab consists of 63 HP and Acer MultiCores workstations Two laser printers for classwork purposes are also available SH 118B classroom has been built out of part of the J Mack Adams lab, and has 40 HP notebooks running 64bit Suse Linux The classroom also has three fixed LCD projectors which project onto a writeable surface and are controlled from an instructor’s console The graduate student lab has high-end Intel machines running 64 bit Suse Linux, and laser printing facilities Many graduate students also share computing resources with their advising faculty members in special-purpose laboratories In addition, every graduate student with an office has one Windows, Mac or Linux host for access to the shared computing facilities of the department The research facilities of the department consist of a great variety of machines located in faculty offices, graduate and special purpose labs These include many PC-based platforms (running a variety of operating systems), as well as several special-purpose parallel computing platforms including a Sun v890 SMP, multi-processor Sun workstations, small clusters and a large cluster consiting of 192 processor cores The Computer Operations Group (COG) operates the department’s computing facilities A large body of software is installed and maintained by this group, and direct support is provided for research projects through identification, acquisition, installation and consulting for a wide variety of software and hardware products

Text: The Computer Science Department facilities have evolved from a single mainframe computing environment to a heterogeneous system of distributed workstations The department has workstations and servers running Linux, Solaris, MacOS, and Windows all connected by a segmented Gigabit ethernet network The J Mack Adams undergraduate lab is based on high-end PC hardware running 64bit Linux operating system At present, the lab consists of 63 HP and Acer MultiCores workstations Two laser printers for classwork purposes are also available SH 118B classroom has been built out of part of the J Mack Adams lab, and has 40 HP notebooks running 64bit Suse Linux The classroom also has three fixed LCD projectors which project onto a writeable surface and are controlled from an instructor’s console The graduate student lab has high-end Intel machines running 64 bit Suse Linux, and laser printing facilities Many graduate students also share computing resources with their advising faculty members in special-purpose laboratories In addition, every graduate student with an office has one Windows, Mac or Linux host for access to the shared computing facilities of the department The research facilities of the department consist of a great variety of machines located in faculty offices, graduate and special purpose labs These include many PC-based platforms (running a variety of operating systems), as well as several special-purpose parallel computing platforms including a Sun v890 SMP, multi-processor Sun workstations, small clusters and a large cluster consiting of 192 processor cores The Computer Operations Group (COG) operates the department’s computing facilities A large body of software is installed and maintained by this group, and direct support is provided for research projects through identification, acquisition, installation and consulting for a wide variety of software and hardware products

Text: The Computer Science Department facilities have evolved from a single mainframe computing environment to a heterogeneous system of distributed workstations The department has workstations and servers running Linux, Solaris, MacOS, and Windows all connected by a segmented Gigabit ethernet network The J Mack Adams undergraduate lab is based on high-end PC hardware running 64bit Linux operating system At present, the lab consists of 63 HP and Acer MultiCores workstations Two laser printers for classwork purposes are also available SH 118B classroom has been built out of part of the J Mack Adams lab, and has 40 HP notebooks running 64bit Suse Linux The classroom also has three fixed LCD projectors which project onto a writeable surface and are controlled from an instructor’s console The graduate student lab has high-end Intel machines running 64 bit Suse Linux, and laser printing facilities Many graduate students also share computing resources with their advising faculty members in special-purpose laboratories In addition, every graduate student with an office has one Windows, Mac or Linux host for access to the shared computing facilities of the department The research facilities of the department consist of a great variety of machines located in faculty offices, graduate and special purpose labs These include many PC-based platforms (running a variety of operating systems), as well as several special-purpose parallel computing platforms including a Sun v890 SMP, multi-processor Sun workstations, small clusters and a large cluster consiting of 192 processor cores The Computer Operations Group (COG) operates the department’s computing facilities A large body of software is installed and maintained by this group, and direct support is provided for research projects through identification, acquisition, installation and consulting for a wide variety of software and hardware products

question: Would I enroll in the same courses whether I am getting a BA or BS in Computer Science?
answer:
No. The B.A. and B.S. in Computer Science share much of the same Computer Science core, but you would not enroll in exactly the same courses for the full degree.

Both degrees include core CS courses such as CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2230 Assembly Language and Machine Organization, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, CSCI 3710 Software Development, CSCI 3730 Compilers and Automata Theory, CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing, CSCI 4140 Database Management Systems I, and a capstone option such as CSCI 4980 Senior Project or CSCI 4999 Senior Thesis.

The B.S. is more structured and more math/science-heavy. It requires MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, MATH 1521G Calculus and Analytic Geometry II or MATH 1521H Calculus and Analytic Geometry II Honors, additional math such as MATH 2415 Introduction to Linear Algebra or MATH 4230 Applied Linear Algebra, another upper-division math option, statistics, and additional lab science coursework. It also makes CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 4105 Programming Language Structure I, and CSCI 4120 Operating Systems I required.

The B.A. is more flexible. It allows either MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I or MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, has more open elective space, and requires two upper-division courses in one non-CS department. Some courses that are required in the B.S. may appear as elective options in the B.A., but they are not necessarily required for the B.A.

So, the early CS courses may look very similar, but the B.S. and B.A. diverge significantly in math, science, upper-division CS requirements, and elective flexibility.

question: Would I enroll in the same courses whether I am getting a BA or BS in Computer Science?
answer:
No. The B.A. and B.S. in Computer Science share much of the same Computer Science core, but you would not enroll in exactly the same courses for the full degree.

Both degrees include core CS courses such as CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2230 Assembly Language and Machine Organization, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, CSCI 3710 Software Development, CSCI 3730 Compilers and Automata Theory, CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing, CSCI 4140 Database Management Systems I, and a capstone option such as CSCI 4980 Senior Project or CSCI 4999 Senior Thesis.

The B.S. is more structured and more math/science-heavy. It requires MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, MATH 1521G Calculus and Analytic Geometry II or MATH 1521H Calculus and Analytic Geometry II Honors, additional math such as MATH 2415 Introduction to Linear Algebra or MATH 4230 Applied Linear Algebra, another upper-division math option, statistics, and additional lab science coursework. It also makes CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 4105 Programming Language Structure I, and CSCI 4120 Operating Systems I required.

The B.A. is more flexible. It allows either MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I or MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, has more open elective space, and requires two upper-division courses in one non-CS department. Some courses that are required in the B.S. may appear as elective options in the B.A., but they are not necessarily required for the B.A.

So, the early CS courses may look very similar, but the B.S. and B.A. diverge significantly in math, science, upper-division CS requirements, and elective flexibility.

question: Would I enroll in the same courses whether I am getting a BA or BS in Computer Science?
answer:
No. The B.A. and B.S. in Computer Science share much of the same Computer Science core, but you would not enroll in exactly the same courses for the full degree.

Both degrees include core CS courses such as CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2230 Assembly Language and Machine Organization, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, CSCI 3710 Software Development, CSCI 3730 Compilers and Automata Theory, CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing, CSCI 4140 Database Management Systems I, and a capstone option such as CSCI 4980 Senior Project or CSCI 4999 Senior Thesis.

The B.S. is more structured and more math/science-heavy. It requires MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, MATH 1521G Calculus and Analytic Geometry II or MATH 1521H Calculus and Analytic Geometry II Honors, additional math such as MATH 2415 Introduction to Linear Algebra or MATH 4230 Applied Linear Algebra, another upper-division math option, statistics, and additional lab science coursework. It also makes CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 4105 Programming Language Structure I, and CSCI 4120 Operating Systems I required.

The B.A. is more flexible. It allows either MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I or MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, has more open elective space, and requires two upper-division courses in one non-CS department. Some courses that are required in the B.S. may appear as elective options in the B.A., but they are not necessarily required for the B.A.

So, the early CS courses may look very similar, but the B.S. and B.A. diverge significantly in math, science, upper-division CS requirements, and elective flexibility.

Text: How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: Would I enroll in the same courses whether I am getting a BA or BS in Computer Science?
answer:
No. The B.A. and B.S. in Computer Science share much of the same Computer Science core, but you would not enroll in exactly the same courses for the full degree.

Both degrees include core CS courses such as CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2230 Assembly Language and Machine Organization, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, CSCI 3710 Software Development, CSCI 3730 Compilers and Automata Theory, CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing, CSCI 4140 Database Management Systems I, and a capstone option such as CSCI 4980 Senior Project or CSCI 4999 Senior Thesis.

The B.S. is more structured and more math/science-heavy. It requires MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, MATH 1521G Calculus and Analytic Geometry II or MATH 1521H Calculus and Analytic Geometry II Honors, additional math such as MATH 2415 Introduction to Linear Algebra or MATH 4230 Applied Linear Algebra, another upper-division math option, statistics, and additional lab science coursework. It also makes CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 4105 Programming Language Structure I, and CSCI 4120 Operating Systems I required.

The B.A. is more flexible. It allows either MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I or MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, has more open elective space, and requires two upper-division courses in one non-CS department. Some courses that are required in the B.S. may appear as elective options in the B.A., but they are not necessarily required for the B.A.

So, the early CS courses may look very similar, but the B.S. and B.A. diverge significantly in math, science, upper-division CS requirements, and elective flexibility.

question: Would I enroll in the same courses whether I am getting a BA or BS in Computer Science?
answer:
No. The B.A. and B.S. in Computer Science share much of the same Computer Science core, but you would not enroll in exactly the same courses for the full degree.

Both degrees include core CS courses such as CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2230 Assembly Language and Machine Organization, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, CSCI 3710 Software Development, CSCI 3730 Compilers and Automata Theory, CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing, CSCI 4140 Database Management Systems I, and a capstone option such as CSCI 4980 Senior Project or CSCI 4999 Senior Thesis.

The B.S. is more structured and more math/science-heavy. It requires MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, MATH 1521G Calculus and Analytic Geometry II or MATH 1521H Calculus and Analytic Geometry II Honors, additional math such as MATH 2415 Introduction to Linear Algebra or MATH 4230 Applied Linear Algebra, another upper-division math option, statistics, and additional lab science coursework. It also makes CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 4105 Programming Language Structure I, and CSCI 4120 Operating Systems I required.

The B.A. is more flexible. It allows either MATH 1430G Applications of Calculus I or MATH 1511G Calculus and Analytic Geometry I, has more open elective space, and requires two upper-division courses in one non-CS department. Some courses that are required in the B.S. may appear as elective options in the B.A., but they are not necessarily required for the B.A.

So, the early CS courses may look very similar, but the B.S. and B.A. diverge significantly in math, science, upper-division CS requirements, and elective flexibility.

question: What courses can I take after taking CSCI 2310?
answer:
If you mean the B.S. in Computer Science suggested plan, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science appears in the sophomore year. The CS courses shown after that point in the suggested plan are:

Sophomore year: CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms and CSCI 3730 Compilers and Automata Theory.

Junior year: CSCI 3710 Software Development, CSCI 4105 Programming Language Structure I, CSCI 4140 Database Management Systems I, and a Computer Science 4000-level elective.

Senior year: CSCI 4980 Senior Project or CSCI 4999 Senior Thesis, CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing, and CSCI 4120 Operating Systems I.

This is the suggested sequencing for the B.S. in Computer Science, not a full prerequisite clearance list. Seat availability for a specific semester or section has to be checked in NMSU course search: https://banner-public.nmsu.edu/StudentRegistrationSsb/ssb/term/termSelection?mode=search. Select the semester, then filter Subject: CSCI, Campus: Las Cruces.

You should receive instructions from graduate school on this. Please make sure not to miss the deadline. Discuss with your project/thesis advisor to form a committee (at least two CS faculty and one non-CS faculty). Fill in the “program of study” form, which can be downloaded from this link; ask you advisor, the department head, and the college dean to sign the form; send the form to graduate school. Schedule your final exam, fill in the Master’s final exam form (which can be downloaded from here), and send it to graduate school. Note that the deadlines to defend a project and a thesis is different. You need to check graduate school regulations on this. Finish and send your project report/thesis to your committee at least one week before the exam. Different advisors may have slightly different requirements; you need to discuss this with your project/thesis advisor. Defend. The defense generally lasts about 1.5 hours where you need to present your project/thesis (about 30 minutes), answer questions specific to your project/thesis, and answer coursework related questions.

Problems and Complaints If you have a problem you would like to sort out or a complaint to make, with regard to the department’s graduate program, examinations, procedures and so on, you are strongly encouraged to consult an appropriate member of the faculty. Of course, you will typically want to talk about it with other students, but please be aware that in the past some graduate students have received seriously wrong impressions or advice through relying entirely on other students. It’s usually best to talk first with your Advisor. It’s also a good idea to consult the graduate student who is currently designated the Graduate Student Representative to the faculty (typically, this person is the same as the President of the CS Graduate Students Organization). The next step is probably to talk to the Graduate Committee Chair. Part of the function of this committee is to help you with problems. Finally, if none of these avenues takes you anywhere useful, you are encouraged to speak to the Department Head. Normally you should exhaust the help the department can provide before consulting other bodies in the university. The immediate next level is the Office of the Dean of the College of Arts & Sciences. Q106. What is the procedure to graduate with Master’s project/thesis ? A. The steps for graduation are: In the semester that you plan to graduate, make sure to apply for graduation & degree. You should receive instructions from graduate school on this. Please make sure not to miss the deadline. Discuss with your project/thesis advisor to form a committee (at least two CS faculty and one non-CS faculty). Fill in the “program of study” form, which can be downloaded from this link; ask you advisor, the department head, and the college dean to sign the form; send the form to graduate school. Schedule your final exam, fill in the Master’s final exam form (which can be downloaded from here), and send it to graduate school. Note that the deadlines to defend a project and a thesis is different. You need to check graduate school regulations on this. Finish and send your project report/thesis to your committee at least one week before the exam. Different advisors may have slightly different requirements; you need to discuss this with your project/thesis advisor. Defend. The defense generally lasts about 1.5 hours where you need to present your project/thesis (about 30 minutes), answer questions specific to your project/thesis, and answer coursework related questions.

Text: Policies & Procedures
Problems and Complaints If you have a problem you would like to sort out or a complaint to make, with regard to the department’s graduate program, examinations, procedures and so on, you are strongly encouraged to consult an appropriate member of the faculty. Of course, you will typically want to talk about it with other students, but please be aware that in the past some graduate students have received seriously wrong impressions or advice through relying entirely on other students. It’s usually best to talk first with your Advisor. It’s also a good idea to consult the graduate student who is currently designated the Graduate Student Representative to the faculty (typically, this person is the same as the President of the CS Graduate Students Organization). The next step is probably to talk to the Graduate Committee Chair. Part of the function of this committee is to help you with problems. Finally, if none of these avenues takes you anywhere useful, you are encouraged to speak to the Department Head. Normally you should exhaust the help the department can provide before consulting other bodies in the university. The immediate next level is the Office of the Dean of the College of Arts & Sciences. Straightforward procedural questions should be taken first to the department office personnel. Office Space The department typically assigns shared office space to students who are supported by Teaching or Research Assistantships. Office space will be granted based on demand and availability. Students are required to return office keys at the end of each semester.

Text: Research Facilities The University recognizes and supports the concept of off-campus study and research as a valuable experience for graduate students. These experiences may take the form of internships, intensive study of specialized techniques with personnel at other institutions, and the conducting of research at specialized research facilities. Arrangements for such off-campus activities should be made with the student’s committee and the graduate dean and should represent opportunities not normally available at this university. When the bulk of a student’s research is to be conducted off-campus, both on- and off-campus advisors should be appointed and periodic meetings with the student’s committee held to ensure timely progress. Students are encouraged to pursue these opportunities with their advisors and the graduate dean.

question: What do I need to do in order to get my masters degree in CS?
answer:
To earn the Master of Science in Computer Science, you need to complete the required graduate coursework and choose either the thesis/project track or the coursework-only track.

All MS CS students must complete 12 credits of basic requirements: one Basic course, one Theories course, one Systems course, and one Applications course. The Basic requirement is CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition or CSCI 5505 Analysis of Algorithms. Students who earned a B or better in CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms are not required to take CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition.

For the thesis/project track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement, 15 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000, and 6 credits of either CSCI 5999 Master’s Thesis or CSCI 5994 Master’s Project. This track also requires a master’s final exam covering both the thesis or project and graduate coursework.

For the coursework-only track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement plus 24 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000. This track does not include the thesis/project requirement.

Some restrictions apply. A course can satisfy only one requirement. For thesis/project students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics and up to 6 credits of CSCI 5991 Special Research Problems may count toward the degree, and no course numbered above 5999 may count. For coursework-only students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics may count, and no course numbered above 5888 may count. Non-CS courses can be included only with prior written approval from your advisor and the departmental Graduate Committee.

If you are doing the thesis or project track, during the semester you plan to graduate you also need to apply for graduation, form a committee with your advisor, submit the program of study form, schedule the final exam, send your project report or thesis to your committee at least one week before the exam, and defend your work.

If you have not yet been admitted, you can begin the application process at https://apply.nmsu.edu/apply. Application materials include transcripts, a personal statement, English test results for international students, and names of three reference providers.

question: What do I need to do in order to get my masters degree in CS?
answer:
To earn the Master of Science in Computer Science, you need to complete the required graduate coursework and choose either the thesis/project track or the coursework-only track.

All MS CS students must complete 12 credits of basic requirements: one Basic course, one Theories course, one Systems course, and one Applications course. The Basic requirement is CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition or CSCI 5505 Analysis of Algorithms. Students who earned a B or better in CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms are not required to take CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition.

For the thesis/project track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement, 15 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000, and 6 credits of either CSCI 5999 Master’s Thesis or CSCI 5994 Master’s Project. This track also requires a master’s final exam covering both the thesis or project and graduate coursework.

For the coursework-only track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement plus 24 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000. This track does not include the thesis/project requirement.

Some restrictions apply. A course can satisfy only one requirement. For thesis/project students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics and up to 6 credits of CSCI 5991 Special Research Problems may count toward the degree, and no course numbered above 5999 may count. For coursework-only students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics may count, and no course numbered above 5888 may count. Non-CS courses can be included only with prior written approval from your advisor and the departmental Graduate Committee.

If you are doing the thesis or project track, during the semester you plan to graduate you also need to apply for graduation, form a committee with your advisor, submit the program of study form, schedule the final exam, send your project report or thesis to your committee at least one week before the exam, and defend your work.

If you have not yet been admitted, you can begin the application process at https://apply.nmsu.edu/apply. Application materials include transcripts, a personal statement, English test results for international students, and names of three reference providers.

Q106. What is the procedure to graduate with Master’s project/thesis ? A. The steps for graduation are: In the semester that you plan to graduate, make sure to apply for graduation & degree. You should receive instructions from graduate school on this. Please make sure not to miss the deadline. Discuss with your project/thesis advisor to form a committee (at least two CS faculty and one non-CS faculty). Fill in the “program of study” form, which can be downloaded from this link; ask you advisor, the department head, and the college dean to sign the form; send the form to graduate school. Schedule your final exam, fill in the Master’s final exam form (which can be downloaded from here), and send it to graduate school. Note that the deadlines to defend a project and a thesis is different. You need to check graduate school regulations on this. Different advisors may have slightly different requirements; you need to discuss this with your project/thesis advisor. Defend. question: What do I need to do in order to get my masters degree in CS?
answer:
To earn the Master of Science in Computer Science, you need to complete the required graduate coursework and choose either the thesis/project track or the coursework-only track.

All MS CS students must complete 12 credits of basic requirements: one Basic course, one Theories course, one Systems course, and one Applications course. The Basic requirement is CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition or CSCI 5505 Analysis of Algorithms. Students who earned a B or better in CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms are not required to take CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition.

For the thesis/project track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement, 15 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000, and 6 credits of either CSCI 5999 Master’s Thesis or CSCI 5994 Master’s Project. This track also requires a master’s final exam covering both the thesis or project and graduate coursework.

For the coursework-only track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement plus 24 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000. This track does not include the thesis/project requirement.

Some restrictions apply. A course can satisfy only one requirement. For thesis/project students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics and up to 6 credits of CSCI 5991 Special Research Problems may count toward the degree, and no course numbered above 5999 may count. For coursework-only students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics may count, and no course numbered above 5888 may count. Non-CS courses can be included only with prior written approval from your advisor and the departmental Graduate Committee.

If you are doing the thesis or project track, during the semester you plan to graduate you also need to apply for graduation, form a committee with your advisor, submit the program of study form, schedule the final exam, send your project report or thesis to your committee at least one week before the exam, and defend your work.

If you have not yet been admitted, you can begin the application process at https://apply.nmsu.edu/apply. Application materials include transcripts, a personal statement, English test results for international students, and names of three reference providers.

question: What do I need to do in order to get my masters degree in CS?
answer:
To earn the Master of Science in Computer Science, you need to complete the required graduate coursework and choose either the thesis/project track or the coursework-only track.

All MS CS students must complete 12 credits of basic requirements: one Basic course, one Theories course, one Systems course, and one Applications course. The Basic requirement is CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition or CSCI 5505 Analysis of Algorithms. Students who earned a B or better in CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms are not required to take CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition.

For the thesis/project track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement, 15 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000, and 6 credits of either CSCI 5999 Master’s Thesis or CSCI 5994 Master’s Project. This track also requires a master’s final exam covering both the thesis or project and graduate coursework.

For the coursework-only track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement plus 24 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000. This track does not include the thesis/project requirement.

Some restrictions apply. A course can satisfy only one requirement. For thesis/project students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics and up to 6 credits of CSCI 5991 Special Research Problems may count toward the degree, and no course numbered above 5999 may count. For coursework-only students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics may count, and no course numbered above 5888 may count. Non-CS courses can be included only with prior written approval from your advisor and the departmental Graduate Committee.

If you are doing the thesis or project track, during the semester you plan to graduate you also need to apply for graduation, form a committee with your advisor, submit the program of study form, schedule the final exam, send your project report or thesis to your committee at least one week before the exam, and defend your work.

If you have not yet been admitted, you can begin the application process at https://apply.nmsu.edu/apply. Application materials include transcripts, a personal statement, English test results for international students, and names of three reference providers.

question: What do I need to do in order to get my masters degree in CS?
answer:
To earn the Master of Science in Computer Science, you need to complete the required graduate coursework and choose either the thesis/project track or the coursework-only track.

All MS CS students must complete 12 credits of basic requirements: one Basic course, one Theories course, one Systems course, and one Applications course. The Basic requirement is CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition or CSCI 5505 Analysis of Algorithms. Students who earned a B or better in CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms are not required to take CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition.

For the thesis/project track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement, 15 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000, and 6 credits of either CSCI 5999 Master’s Thesis or CSCI 5994 Master’s Project. This track also requires a master’s final exam covering both the thesis or project and graduate coursework.

For the coursework-only track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement plus 24 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000. This track does not include the thesis/project requirement.

Some restrictions apply. A course can satisfy only one requirement. For thesis/project students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics and up to 6 credits of CSCI 5991 Special Research Problems may count toward the degree, and no course numbered above 5999 may count. For coursework-only students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics may count, and no course numbered above 5888 may count. Non-CS courses can be included only with prior written approval from your advisor and the departmental Graduate Committee.

If you are doing the thesis or project track, during the semester you plan to graduate you also need to apply for graduation, form a committee with your advisor, submit the program of study form, schedule the final exam, send your project report or thesis to your committee at least one week before the exam, and defend your work.

If you have not yet been admitted, you can begin the application process at https://apply.nmsu.edu/apply. Application materials include transcripts, a personal statement, English test results for international students, and names of three reference providers.

question: What do I need to do in order to get my masters degree in CS?
answer:
To earn the Master of Science in Computer Science, you need to complete the required graduate coursework and choose either the thesis/project track or the coursework-only track.

All MS CS students must complete 12 credits of basic requirements: one Basic course, one Theories course, one Systems course, and one Applications course. The Basic requirement is CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition or CSCI 5505 Analysis of Algorithms. Students who earned a B or better in CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms are not required to take CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition.

For the thesis/project track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement, 15 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000, and 6 credits of either CSCI 5999 Master’s Thesis or CSCI 5994 Master’s Project. This track also requires a master’s final exam covering both the thesis or project and graduate coursework.

For the coursework-only track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement plus 24 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000. This track does not include the thesis/project requirement.

Some restrictions apply. A course can satisfy only one requirement. For thesis/project students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics and up to 6 credits of CSCI 5991 Special Research Problems may count toward the degree, and no course numbered above 5999 may count. For coursework-only students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics may count, and no course numbered above 5888 may count. Non-CS courses can be included only with prior written approval from your advisor and the departmental Graduate Committee.

If you are doing the thesis or project track, during the semester you plan to graduate you also need to apply for graduation, form a committee with your advisor, submit the program of study form, schedule the final exam, send your project report or thesis to your committee at least one week before the exam, and defend your work.

If you have not yet been admitted, you can begin the application process at https://apply.nmsu.edu/apply. Application materials include transcripts, a personal statement, English test results for international students, and names of three reference providers.
