question: What do I need to do in order to get my masters degree in CS?
answer:
To earn the Master of Science in Computer Science, you need to complete the required graduate coursework and choose either the thesis/project track or the coursework-only track.

All MS CS students must complete 12 credits of basic requirements: one Basic course, one Theories course, one Systems course, and one Applications course. The Basic requirement is CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition or CSCI 5505 Analysis of Algorithms. Students who earned a B or better in CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms are not required to take CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition.

For the thesis/project track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement, 15 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000, and 6 credits of either CSCI 5999 Master’s Thesis or CSCI 5994 Master’s Project. This track also requires a master’s final exam covering both the thesis or project and graduate coursework.

For the coursework-only track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement plus 24 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000. This track does not include the thesis/project requirement.

Some restrictions apply. A course can satisfy only one requirement. For thesis/project students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics and up to 6 credits of CSCI 5991 Special Research Problems may count toward the degree, and no course numbered above 5999 may count. For coursework-only students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics may count, and no course numbered above 5888 may count. Non-CS courses can be included only with prior written approval from your advisor and the departmental Graduate Committee.

If you are doing the thesis or project track, during the semester you plan to graduate you also need to apply for graduation, form a committee with your advisor, submit the program of study form, schedule the final exam, send your project report or thesis to your committee at least one week before the exam, and defend your work.

If you have not yet been admitted, you can begin the application process at https://apply.nmsu.edu/apply. Application materials include transcripts, a personal statement, English test results for international students, and names of three reference providers.

question: What do I need to do in order to get my masters degree in CS?
answer:
To earn the Master of Science in Computer Science, you need to complete the required graduate coursework and choose either the thesis/project track or the coursework-only track.

All MS CS students must complete 12 credits of basic requirements: one Basic course, one Theories course, one Systems course, and one Applications course. The Basic requirement is CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition or CSCI 5505 Analysis of Algorithms. Students who earned a B or better in CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms are not required to take CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition.

For the thesis/project track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement, 15 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000, and 6 credits of either CSCI 5999 Master’s Thesis or CSCI 5994 Master’s Project. This track also requires a master’s final exam covering both the thesis or project and graduate coursework.

question: What do I need to do in order to get my masters degree in CS?
answer:
To earn the Master of Science in Computer Science, you need to complete the required graduate coursework and choose either the thesis/project track or the coursework-only track.

All MS CS students must complete 12 credits of basic requirements: one Basic course, one Theories course, one Systems course, and one Applications course. The Basic requirement is CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition or CSCI 5505 Analysis of Algorithms. Students who earned a B or better in CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms are not required to take CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition.

For the thesis/project track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement, 15 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000, and 6 credits of either CSCI 5999 Master’s Thesis or CSCI 5994 Master’s Project. This track also requires a master’s final exam covering both the thesis or project and graduate coursework.

For the coursework-only track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement plus 24 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000. This track does not include the thesis/project requirement.

Some restrictions apply. A course can satisfy only one requirement. For thesis/project students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics and up to 6 credits of CSCI 5991 Special Research Problems may count toward the degree, and no course numbered above 5999 may count. For coursework-only students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics may count, and no course numbered above 5888 may count. Non-CS courses can be included only with prior written approval from your advisor and the departmental Graduate Committee.

If you are doing the thesis or project track, during the semester you plan to graduate you also need to apply for graduation, form a committee with your advisor, submit the program of study form, schedule the final exam, send your project report or thesis to your committee at least one week before the exam, and defend your work.

If you have not yet been admitted, you can begin the application process at https://apply.nmsu.edu/apply. Application materials include transcripts, a personal statement, English test results for international students, and names of three reference providers.

question: What do I need to do in order to get my masters degree in CS?
answer:
To earn the Master of Science in Computer Science, you need to complete the required graduate coursework and choose either the thesis/project track or the coursework-only track.

All MS CS students must complete 12 credits of basic requirements: one Basic course, one Theories course, one Systems course, and one Applications course. The Basic requirement is CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition or CSCI 5505 Analysis of Algorithms. Students who earned a B or better in CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms are not required to take CSCI 5110 Data Structure and Algorithms Transition.

For the thesis/project track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement, 15 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000, and 6 credits of either CSCI 5999 Master’s Thesis or CSCI 5994 Master’s Project. This track also requires a master’s final exam covering both the thesis or project and graduate coursework.

For the coursework-only track, you must complete the 12-credit basic requirement plus 24 additional credits of Computer Science graduate courses numbered above 5000. This track does not include the thesis/project requirement.

Some restrictions apply. A course can satisfy only one requirement. For thesis/project students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics and up to 6 credits of CSCI 5991 Special Research Problems may count toward the degree, and no course numbered above 5999 may count. For coursework-only students, up to 6 credits of CSCI 5996 Special Topics may count, and no course numbered above 5888 may count. Non-CS courses can be included only with prior written approval from your advisor and the departmental Graduate Committee.

If you are doing the thesis or project track, during the semester you plan to graduate you also need to apply for graduation, form a committee with your advisor, submit the program of study form, schedule the final exam, send your project report or thesis to your committee at least one week before the exam, and defend your work.

If you have not yet been admitted, you can begin the application process at https://apply.nmsu.edu/apply. Application materials include transcripts, a personal statement, English test results for international students, and names of three reference providers.

text: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is the traditional undergraduate degree in Computer Science. text: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is the traditional undergraduate degree in Computer Science. It is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of Computer Science. It prepares the student for any technological ﬁeld in industry, and also provides the preparation for graduate studies in Computer Science. It is the main undergraduate degree in the Computer Science department, and should be the choice of a single-major Computer Science student. This degree is accredited by the ABET Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria. General Requirements Exception A grade of at least C- must be earned in each of the courses taken to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. No course may be counted as satisfying both a departmental and a non-departmental requirement. No course taken to satisfy either a departmental or a non-departmental requirement may be taken S/U. Requirements Students who plan to seek employment at the bachelor level are advised to take one of the concentration area curricula in addition to the general and departmental requirements. An elective course cannot be used for more than two focuses. A course that is required for one concentration cannot be used as an elective course of another one. Students must complete all University degree requirements, which include: General Education requirements, Viewing a Wider World requirements, and elective credits to total at least 120 credits with 48 credits in courses numbered 300/3000 or above. Developmental coursework will not count towards the degree requirements and/or elective credits, but may be needed in order to take the necessary English and Mathematics coursework. question: What is the minimum GPA for greaduation in BS CS program?
answer:

answer:
For the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science, a specific minimum graduation GPA is not available in the provided department sources.

What is specified is that you must earn at least a C- in each course used to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. The degree also requires at least 120 total credits, including 48 credits in courses numbered 300/3000 or above, along with all university degree requirements.

Text: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is the traditional undergraduate degree in Computer Science. It is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of Computer Science. It prepares the student for any technological ﬁeld in industry, and also provides the preparation for graduate studies in Computer Science. It is the main undergraduate degree in the Computer Science department, and should be the choice of a single-major Computer Science student. This degree is accredited by the ABET Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria. General Requirements Exception A grade of at least C- must be earned in each of the courses taken to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. No course may be counted as satisfying both a departmental and a non-departmental requirement. No course taken to satisfy either a departmental or a non-departmental requirement may be taken S/U. Requirements Students who plan to seek employment at the bachelor level are advised to take one of the concentration area curricula in addition to the general and departmental requirements. An elective course cannot be used for more than two focuses. A course that is required for one concentration cannot be used as an elective course of another one. Students must complete all University degree requirements, which include: General Education requirements, Viewing a Wider World requirements, and elective credits to total at least 120 credits with 48 credits in courses numbered 300 or above. Developmental coursework will not count towards the degree requirements and/or elective credits, but may be needed in order to take the necessary English and Mathematics coursework. question: What is the minimum GPA for greaduation in BS CS program?
answer:
For the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science, a specific minimum graduation GPA is not available in the provided department sources.

What is specified is that you must earn at least a C- in each course used to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. The degree also requires at least 120 total credits, including 48 credits in courses numbered 300/3000 or above, along with all university degree requirements.

Text: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is the traditional undergraduate degree in Computer Science. It is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of Computer Science. It prepares the student for any technological ﬁeld in industry, and also provides the preparation for graduate studies in Computer Science. It is the main undergraduate degree in the Computer Science department, and should be the choice of a single-major Computer Science student. This degree is accredited by the ABET Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria. General Requirements Exception A grade of at least C- must be earned in each of the courses taken to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. No course may be counted as satisfying both a departmental and a non-departmental requirement. No course taken to satisfy either a departmental or a non-departmental requirement may be taken S/U. Requirements Students who plan to seek employment at the bachelor level are advised to take one of the concentration area curricula in addition to the general and departmental requirements. An elective course cannot be used for more than two focuses. A course that is required for one concentration cannot be used as an elective course of another one. Students must complete all University degree requirements, which include: General Education requirements, Viewing a Wider World requirements, and elective credits to total at least 120 credits with 48 credits in courses numbered 300 or above. Developmental coursework will not count towards the degree requirements and/or elective credits, but may be needed in order to take the necessary English and Mathematics coursework. Text: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is the traditional undergraduate degree in Computer Science. It is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of Computer Science. It prepares the student for any technological ﬁeld in industry, and also provides the preparation for graduate studies in Computer Science. It is the main undergraduate degree in the Computer Science department, and should be the choice of a single-major Computer Science student. This degree is accredited by the ABET Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria. General Requirements Exception A grade of at least C- must be earned in each of the courses taken to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. No course may be counted as satisfying both a departmental and a non-departmental requirement. No course taken to satisfy either a departmental or a non-departmental requirement may be taken S/U. Requirements Students who plan to seek employment at the bachelor level are advised to take one of the concentration area curricula in addition to the general and departmental requirements. An elective course cannot be used for more than two focuses. A course that is required for one concentration cannot be used as an elective course of another one. Students must complete all University degree requirements, which include: General Education requirements, Viewing a Wider World requirements, and elective credits to total at least 120 credits with 48 credits in courses numbered 300 or above. Developmental coursework will not count towards the degree requirements and/or elective credits, but may be needed in order to take the necessary English and Mathematics coursework. question: What is the minimum GPA for greaduation in BS CS program?
answer:
For the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science, a specific minimum graduation GPA is not available in the provided department sources.

What is specified is that you must earn at least a C- in each course used to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. The degree also requires at least 120 total credits, including 48 credits in courses numbered 300/3000 or above, along with all university degree requirements.

Text: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is the traditional undergraduate degree in Computer Science. It is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of Computer Science. It prepares the student for any technological ﬁeld in industry, and also provides the preparation for graduate studies in Computer Science. It is the main undergraduate degree in the Computer Science department, and should be the choice of a single-major Computer Science student. This degree is accredited by the ABET Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria. General Requirements Exception A grade of at least C- must be earned in each of the courses taken to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. No course may be counted as satisfying both a departmental and a non-departmental requirement. No course taken to satisfy either a departmental or a non-departmental requirement may be taken S/U. Requirements Students who plan to seek employment at the bachelor level are advised to take one of the concentration area curricula in addition to the general and departmental requirements. An elective course cannot be used for more than two focuses. A course that is required for one concentration cannot be used as an elective course of another one. Students must complete all University degree requirements, which include: General Education requirements, Viewing a Wider World requirements, and elective credits to total at least 120 credits with 48 credits in courses numbered 300 or above. Developmental coursework will not count towards the degree requirements and/or elective credits, but may be needed in order to take the necessary English and Mathematics coursework. question: What is the minimum GPA for greaduation in BS CS program?
answer:
For the Bachelor of Science in Computer Science, a specific minimum graduation GPA is not available in the provided department sources.

What is specified is that you must earn at least a C- in each course used to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. The degree also requires at least 120 total credits, including 48 credits in courses numbered 300/3000 or above, along with all university degree requirements.

Text: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is the traditional undergraduate degree in Computer Science. It is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of Computer Science. It prepares the student for any technological ﬁeld in industry, and also provides the preparation for graduate studies in Computer Science. It is the main undergraduate degree in the Computer Science department, and should be the choice of a single-major Computer Science student. This degree is accredited by the ABET Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria. General Requirements Exception A grade of at least C- must be earned in each of the courses taken to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. No course may be counted as satisfying both a departmental and a non-departmental requirement. No course taken to satisfy either a departmental or a non-departmental requirement may be taken S/U. Requirements Students who plan to seek employment at the bachelor level are advised to take one of the concentration area curricula in addition to the general and departmental requirements. An elective course cannot be used for more than two focuses. A course that is required for one concentration cannot be used as an elective course of another one. Students must complete all University degree requirements, which include: General Education requirements, Viewing a Wider World requirements, and elective credits to total at least 120 credits with 48 credits in courses numbered 300 or above. Developmental coursework will not count towards the degree requirements and/or elective credits, but may be needed in order to take the necessary English and Mathematics coursework. question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

Text: How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

Text: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is the traditional undergraduate degree in Computer Science. It is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of Computer Science. It prepares the student for any technological ﬁeld in industry, and also provides the preparation for graduate studies in Computer Science. It is the main undergraduate degree in the Computer Science department, and should be the choice of a single-major Computer Science student. This degree is accredited by the ABET Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria. General Requirements Exception A grade of at least C- must be earned in each of the courses taken to satisfy the departmental and non-departmental requirements. No course may be counted as satisfying both a departmental and a non-departmental requirement. No course taken to satisfy either a departmental or a non-departmental requirement may be taken S/U. Requirements Students who plan to seek employment at the bachelor level are advised to take one of the concentration area curricula in addition to the general and departmental requirements. An elective course cannot be used for more than two focuses. A course that is required for one concentration cannot be used as an elective course of another one. Students must complete all University degree requirements, which include: General Education requirements, Viewing a Wider World requirements, and elective credits to total at least 120 credits with 48 credits in courses numbered 300/3000 or above. Developmental coursework will not count towards the degree requirements and/or elective credits, but may be needed in order to take the necessary English and Mathematics coursework. question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

heading: How to Select Between the B.S. and B.A.?
text:
How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

Text: How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

Text: How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

Text: How to Select Between the B.S and B.A.?
The B.S in Computer Science is the traditional computer science degree program, which is heavy on the science and math side (as all bachelor in science degrees are) As a B.S degree, it is fairly tightly constrained in terms of fitting its requirements into the 120 credit overall requirement, and so students need to be very careful that the non-CS courses they are choosing fit into the various slots that need filled for the degree It is ABET-CAC accredited and should be your default choice if you have no reason to choose otherwise, and it should be your choice if you are at all considering graduate school The B.S in Cybersecurity is a new degree with a strong focus on preparing students for a career in the cybersecurity industry It is more constrained in terms of courses than the B.S in Computer Science, with students needing to take a specific set of upper division courses that focus on cybersecurity topics The B.S in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a new degree that is rigorously focused on educating the student in the fundamental disciplines of AI The B.A in Computer Science is designed as an innovative open degree program, where you have much more open credit to use for your own educational design This degree is intended for students that have interests outside computer science and want the open credit to use to study other disciplines in some depth It is a great degree to use in a double major, but you do not need to do a full double major to take advantage of its open plan We strongly encourage you to at least have one minor in another department to distinguish yourself and your capabilities ABET statement: The Bachelor of Science in Computer Science is accredited by the Computing Accreditation Commission (CAC) of the ABET , under the General and Computer Science Program Criteria

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

heading: What are the B.S. degree concentrations and how do I choose one?
text:
What are the B.S. degree concentrations and how do I choose one?
The B.S. degree recently added seven areas of concentration. All of these are optional, but will show up on your transcript and diploma if you choose one and satisfy its requirements (specific CS elective course choices). Their requirements are hard to read in the catalog, but if you choose one of the concentrations in the catalog and scroll down to the bottom of the page, there is a table portion with a sentence above it currently reading “Students who plan to seek employment at the bachelor level are advised to use their elective credits to complete the concentration coursework below” — it is the requirements below this that determine the concentration’s requirements.

question: How does the BS CS concentration in AI differ from the BS in AI?
answer:
The main difference is that the B.S. in Computer Science with an Artificial Intelligence concentration is still a Computer Science degree, while the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a separate AI degree.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

The B.S. in Computer Science is described as the traditional undergraduate Computer Science degree, focused on the fundamental disciplines of computer science and preparation for technological fields or graduate study in Computer Science. It is ABET-CAC accredited. The Artificial Intelligence concentration is an optional specialization within that B.S. in Computer Science. Concentrations are completed through specific CS elective choices and can appear on the transcript and diploma if the requirements are satisfied.

For the B.S. in Computer Science concentration in Artificial Intelligence, the concentration-specific coursework includes selecting 3–4 credits from CSCI 3790 Algorithm Design & Implementation or CSCI 3720 Data Structures and Algorithms, plus 9 credits from CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining.

The B.S. in Artificial Intelligence is a standalone 4-year, in-person degree focused on the fundamental disciplines of AI. Its listed requirements include the CS foundation courses CSCI 1720 Computer Science I, CSCI 2210 Object-Oriented Programming, CSCI 2220 Introduction to Data Structures and Algorithms, CSCI 2310 Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science, plus AI-specific and related courses such as CSCI 2410 Practical Programming, CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, CSCI 4405 Artificial Intelligence I, CSCI 4420 Applied Machine Learning I, and CSCI 4415 Introduction to Data Mining. It also includes 12 credits of AI-focused electives, 9 credits of general CS/EE/ICT/BCIS/PSYC courses, and 3 non-departmental credits of math or statistics.

So, in practical terms: choose the CS degree with AI concentration if you want the broader traditional Computer Science degree with an AI specialization. Choose the B.S. in Artificial Intelligence if you want the degree itself to be centered on AI rather than Computer Science with an AI concentration.

question: What computer science courses address computing ethics and governance?
answer:
The strongest match is CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing. It is a 1-credit course covering the history of computing, intellectual property, privacy, ethical frameworks, professional ethical responsibilities, and risks of computer-based systems. It requires at least a C- in CSCI 3710 Software Development.

Other CSCI courses that address related ethics, governance, privacy, or social-impact topics include CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, which includes ethics in agent-based systems and the challenge of ensuring AI agents are safe in society, and CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I, which includes Internet organization and governance topics such as IANA, autonomous systems, internet exchange points, ISPs, certificate authorities, and BGP, along with TLS security and privacy guarantees.

For graduate students, the corresponding graduate networks course is CSCI 5245 Computer Networks I, which covers the same Internet organization and governance topics as CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I but requires more advanced graduate work.

At the introductory level, CSCI 1115G Modern Computing in Practice includes common cybersecurity risks, security, privacy, and societal impacts of technology. CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles also addresses the broader impact of computation and the Internet on society, though it is less directly focused on ethics or governance than CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing.

question: What computer science courses address computing ethics and governance?
answer:
The strongest match is CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing. It is a 1-credit course covering the history of computing, intellectual property, privacy, ethical frameworks, professional ethical responsibilities, and risks of computer-based systems. It requires at least a C- in CSCI 3710 Software Development.

Other CSCI courses that address related ethics, governance, privacy, or social-impact topics include CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, which includes ethics in agent-based systems and the challenge of ensuring AI agents are safe in society, and CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I, which includes Internet organization and governance topics such as IANA, autonomous systems, internet exchange points, ISPs, certificate authorities, and BGP, along with TLS security and privacy guarantees.

For graduate students, the corresponding graduate networks course is CSCI 5245 Computer Networks I, which covers the same Internet organization and governance topics as CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I but requires more advanced graduate work.

At the introductory level, CSCI 1115G Modern Computing in Practice includes common cybersecurity risks, security, privacy, and societal impacts of technology. CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles also addresses the broader impact of computation and the Internet on society, though it is less directly focused on ethics or governance than CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing.

question: What computer science courses address computing ethics and governance?
answer:
The strongest match is CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing. It is a 1-credit course covering the history of computing, intellectual property, privacy, ethical frameworks, professional ethical responsibilities, and risks of computer-based systems. It requires at least a C- in CSCI 3710 Software Development.

Other CSCI courses that address related ethics, governance, privacy, or social-impact topics include CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, which includes ethics in agent-based systems and the challenge of ensuring AI agents are safe in society, and CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I, which includes Internet organization and governance topics such as IANA, autonomous systems, internet exchange points, ISPs, certificate authorities, and BGP, along with TLS security and privacy guarantees.

For graduate students, the corresponding graduate networks course is CSCI 5245 Computer Networks I, which covers the same Internet organization and governance topics as CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I but requires more advanced graduate work.

At the introductory level, CSCI 1115G Modern Computing in Practice includes common cybersecurity risks, security, privacy, and societal impacts of technology. CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles also addresses the broader impact of computation and the Internet on society, though it is less directly focused on ethics or governance than CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing.

question: What computer science courses address computing ethics and governance?
answer:
The strongest match is CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing. It is a 1-credit course covering the history of computing, intellectual property, privacy, ethical frameworks, professional ethical responsibilities, and risks of computer-based systems. It requires at least a C- in CSCI 3710 Software Development.

Other CSCI courses that address related ethics, governance, privacy, or social-impact topics include CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, which includes ethics in agent-based systems and the challenge of ensuring AI agents are safe in society, and CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I, which includes Internet organization and governance topics such as IANA, autonomous systems, internet exchange points, ISPs, certificate authorities, and BGP, along with TLS security and privacy guarantees.

For graduate students, the corresponding graduate networks course is CSCI 5245 Computer Networks I, which covers the same Internet organization and governance topics as CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I but requires more advanced graduate work.

At the introductory level, CSCI 1115G Modern Computing in Practice includes common cybersecurity risks, security, privacy, and societal impacts of technology. CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles also addresses the broader impact of computation and the Internet on society, though it is less directly focused on ethics or governance than CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing.

question: What computer science courses address computing ethics and governance?
answer:
The strongest match is CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing. It is a 1-credit course covering the history of computing, intellectual property, privacy, ethical frameworks, professional ethical responsibilities, and risks of computer-based systems. It requires at least a C- in CSCI 3710 Software Development.

Other CSCI courses that address related ethics, governance, privacy, or social-impact topics include CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, which includes ethics in agent-based systems and the challenge of ensuring AI agents are safe in society, and CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I, which includes Internet organization and governance topics such as IANA, autonomous systems, internet exchange points, ISPs, certificate authorities, and BGP, along with TLS security and privacy guarantees.

For graduate students, the corresponding graduate networks course is CSCI 5245 Computer Networks I, which covers the same Internet organization and governance topics as CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I but requires more advanced graduate work.

At the introductory level, CSCI 1115G Modern Computing in Practice includes common cybersecurity risks, security, privacy, and societal impacts of technology. CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles also addresses the broader impact of computation and the Internet on society, though it is less directly focused on ethics or governance than CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing.

question: What computer science courses address computing ethics and governance?
answer:
The strongest match is CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing. It is a 1-credit course covering the history of computing, intellectual property, privacy, ethical frameworks, professional ethical responsibilities, and risks of computer-based systems. It requires at least a C- in CSCI 3710 Software Development.

Other CSCI courses that address related ethics, governance, privacy, or social-impact topics include CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, which includes ethics in agent-based systems and the challenge of ensuring AI agents are safe in society, and CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I, which includes Internet organization and governance topics such as IANA, autonomous systems, internet exchange points, ISPs, certificate authorities, and BGP, along with TLS security and privacy guarantees.

For graduate students, the corresponding graduate networks course is CSCI 5245 Computer Networks I, which covers the same Internet organization and governance topics as CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I but requires more advanced graduate work.

At the introductory level, CSCI 1115G Modern Computing in Practice includes common cybersecurity risks, security, privacy, and societal impacts of technology. CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles also addresses the broader impact of computation and the Internet on society, though it is less directly focused on ethics or governance than CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing.

question: What computer science courses address computing ethics and governance?
answer:
The strongest match is CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing. It is a 1-credit course covering the history of computing, intellectual property, privacy, ethical frameworks, professional ethical responsibilities, and risks of computer-based systems. It requires at least a C- in CSCI 3710 Software Development.

Other CSCI courses that address related ethics, governance, privacy, or social-impact topics include CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, which includes ethics in agent-based systems and the challenge of ensuring AI agents are safe in society, and CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I, which includes Internet organization and governance topics such as IANA, autonomous systems, internet exchange points, ISPs, certificate authorities, and BGP, along with TLS security and privacy guarantees.

For graduate students, the corresponding graduate networks course is CSCI 5245 Computer Networks I, which covers the same Internet organization and governance topics as CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I but requires more advanced graduate work.

At the introductory level, CSCI 1115G Modern Computing in Practice includes common cybersecurity risks, security, privacy, and societal impacts of technology. CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles also addresses the broader impact of computation and the Internet on society, though it is less directly focused on ethics or governance than CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing.

question: What computer science courses address computing ethics and governance?
answer:
The strongest match is CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing. It is a 1-credit course covering the history of computing, intellectual property, privacy, ethical frameworks, professional ethical responsibilities, and risks of computer-based systems. It requires at least a C- in CSCI 3710 Software Development.

Other CSCI courses that address related ethics, governance, privacy, or social-impact topics include CSCI 3410 Introduction to Intelligent Agents Using Science Fiction, which includes ethics in agent-based systems and the challenge of ensuring AI agents are safe in society, and CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I, which includes Internet organization and governance topics such as IANA, autonomous systems, internet exchange points, ISPs, certificate authorities, and BGP, along with TLS security and privacy guarantees.

For graduate students, the corresponding graduate networks course is CSCI 5245 Computer Networks I, which covers the same Internet organization and governance topics as CSCI 4245 Computer Networks I but requires more advanced graduate work.

At the introductory level, CSCI 1115G Modern Computing in Practice includes common cybersecurity risks, security, privacy, and societal impacts of technology. CSCI 1110 Computer Science Principles also addresses the broader impact of computation and the Internet on society, though it is less directly focused on ethics or governance than CSCI 4110 Computing Ethics and Social Implications of Computing.
